text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Municipal councils in the Stockholm region have received a total of 76 million crowns in subsidies from the European Union.
- Currency speculation could intensify though a fixed exchange rate, such as if Sweden pegs the crown in Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism.
Swedish taxpayers lost 25 billion crowns through the Riksbank's 1992 defence of the crown, which ended in vain.

- One in four Swedish males in secondary education say they never read fiction, choosing instead video films for entertainment. However, fifty percent of girls say they read at least one book per month.

- The fact that the Swedish government refused to cut concession fees for television station TV4 will not dim the horizon for the commercial televison channel, managing director Christer Forsstrom says in an interview.
- Scandinavian Airlines System is among the 10 most profitable airlines in the world. Its profit in 1995 was $370 million, with the industry average at $92 million.
- Sweden has one of the world's largest trade surpluses in relation to gross domestic product. Finland, Denmark and Sweden all have a higher trade surplus/GDP ratio than Japan.

- The first contract for a Swedish company as a direct result of Prime Minister Goran Persson's visit to China has been signed. Information technology firm Frontec won an order for data systems in four Chinese harbours.
